Three water temperature differences were selected: (i) 15 K, (ii) 9 K, and (iii) 7 K, with an inlet temperature of 24°C. The results of this parametric study were compared with those from the A-test manufacturer’s data. To estimate the potential savings using the secondary loop, the theoretical pumping power was calculated using Eq.(11), which is the product of the water volume flow rate and the total pressure drop of both the thermal battery and PHX. Figure 34: Predicted pumping power for the different water temperature differences, mass flow rates, and pump efficiencies Figure 35 compares the COP and power demand with the A-test conditions [50] for the three water temperature differences across the PHX, assuming the lowest pump efficiency. At higher water mass flow rates (i.e., ∆T = 7 K), a 57% increase in COP and a 31% reduction in power consumption were achieved, due to lower compressor temperature lift. To meet this target, simulations were conducted using TMY3 [95] data and building loads from the Spawn of EnergyPlusTM [60], [61] for a DOE prototype small-office building [75]. In these simulations, the building “operating period” was 6 AM to 8 PM, during which continuous space conditioning was required. Table 11 summarizes the utility peak hours for eight representative U.S. cities, one per ASHRAE climate zone.
